Where it began

Rohit Sharma was born on 30 April 1987 in Bansod, Nagpur, and grew up largely in Borivali, Mumbai, in the care of his grandparents and uncles. In 1999 an uncle helped him into a cricket camp, and the coach there, Dinesh Lad, found him a place at Swami Vivekanand International School, where the facilities were better.

At first he was a bowler, sending down off-breaks and batting down at number eight. Lad soon saw where the real talent lay and sent him in to open. He marked the promotion with a century in his first innings at the top of the order.

The player

His Test debut came at Eden Gardens in November 2013, in the series that was Sachin Tendulkar's farewell, and he marked it with 177. In the next match, on his home ground at the Wankhede, he added 111 not out. Few players have ever made a louder entrance.

The real turn came in 2019, when he was asked to open in Tests. In his first match in that role he made a century in each innings against South Africa, and later in the same series he hit his first Test double, 212. In all he played 67 Tests, scoring 4,301 runs at 40.58 with 12 hundreds, and held 68 catches, mostly in the slips. He captained India in 24 Tests and won half of them. He retired from Test cricket in May 2025.

What made him special

He batted with style and elegance, and when he chose to attack, the ball tended to end up in the crowd. That is how he came by the nickname Hitman. His 161 against England in 2021 helped India bounce back after losing the opening Test of the series, and his 127 at The Oval later that year was his first Test hundred away from home.

It took Test cricket a while to see the best of him. For some years he moved in and out of the side, and his finest work came after he went up the order. Once there, he made up for lost time.

Away from the middle

In the shorter formats he holds the highest individual score in one-day internationals, 264, and was captain when India won the T20 World Cup in 2024 and the Champions Trophy in 2025. He has the Arjuna Award, the Khel Ratna and, from 2026, the Padma Shri, and Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year.

He cares a great deal about animals. He has worked with PETA on behalf of street dogs and cats, joined a campaign in Kenya against poaching, and in 2018 became WWF-India's rhino ambassador. After leaving Tests he carried on in one-day cricket for India.

And finally

The off-spinner who first walked into Dinesh Lad's camp never quite went away. He took two Test wickets, at a little over a hundred runs apiece. Both, he would surely say, were worth the wait.
